prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated without Doppler, recoil or light-shift perturbation, bringing frequency measurement to uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B018, Katori and Ye. After the first round the scientific case rests on a distinction I think the citation can make explicit. The 2005 prize recognised the optical frequency comb, the gearbox that counts optical cycles. The 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, which gave the ion clock. The lattice clock is a third thing: a way to hold thousands of neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime at a wavelength where the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that the statistics of an ensemble and the systematic control of a trapped particle are obtained together. Neither earlier prize contains that principle, and it is what allowed stability to improve through averaging over many atoms and let systematic uncertainties go to 1e-18. Reproduction is the evidence I weigh most: Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others have reproduced the performance on Sr and Yb, and inter-laboratory comparisons check the uncertainty budgets. The consequences are already measured, not hypothetical: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on drifts of constants, and dark-matter searches with clock networks. On credit, the exchange has moved me toward a more careful statement, not a weaker one. Katori originated the magic-wavelength lattice and built the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group made it a precision instrument, with the systematic evaluation, laser and coherence work that took it to the 1e-18 level and into the many-body regime. That is a distinct contribution, not a later copy.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 remains the strongest objection, and Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig are right that part of the 1e-18 figure is a metrological record and not a surprise from nature. I answer that the record is only reachable because of the trapping principle, but a member who values discoveries about nature over instruments can weigh it differently, and I do not claim the question is closed. Second, the two-name credit is not as clean as I wrote in round 1. Olsson is right that a later and better realisation is not the original discovery, and Mehlig is right that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups are part of the story and are not covered. I judge that Katori and Ye are the two people without whom the technique would not exist as a precision tool, but the committee should record this and not call it self-evident. Third, I have changed my view on timing: I raised waiting for the redefinition of the second in round 1, but I now think it ties our decision to a metrology calendar and the accuracy results already stand on independent confirmation. I would only wait if an expert reviewer found that the 1e-18 comparisons are not what the supplied files say.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B018, asked whether Ye's share is the accuracy and many-body work or also comb-based infrastructure, since only the first is new relative to 2005, and disagreed with waiting for the SI redefinition.
responses.response: On his question: my answer is that Ye's share for this prize is the first, and the citation should say so. The comb is the readout infrastructure that Hall and Hansch were honoured for, and I do not think Ye's work with the comb should count here. What is specific to Ye is the systematic evaluation of the strontium lattice clock, the ultrastable-laser and coherence work that let long interrogation times be used, and the many-body and spin-correlation regime, which depends on the lattice and not on the comb. I accept his argument about the redefinition, and it changes my position: we should not tie the prize to another body's schedule. I would still ask an expert reviewer to confirm the current record uncertainties and comparisons, since none of us can check them from the files.

responses.point: Olsson moved B018 to her first choice but does not accept that the credit is clean, because Ye improved a concept Katori proposed and the committee has said that a later and better realisation is not the original discovery.
responses.response: She is right to push back on the word clean and I withdraw it. Her proposed remedy, a citation about the lattice clock as a new type of instrument with Katori as originator and Ye as the one who made it a precision tool, is one I can support. I would add a reason why Ye is more than refinement. The first lattice clocks were orders of magnitude from the level where clocks become tools for fundamental physics. Closing that gap meant new understanding of collisional, blackbody and lattice-light-shift systematics, and new ways to keep the atoms coherent, which is original experimental work and not repetition. I would not accept the Ye share if it were framed only as best-ever accuracy. My stated rule is the same as hers, and I think the pair passes it, though not by a wide margin.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts B018 as the most defensible package but sees its payoffs as still prospective, a clock that follows the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says B038 has the larger discovery content.
responses.response: I agree that B038 has more discovery content in the sense he uses, a clue from nature that settled a thirty-year question. My difficulty is the one he states himself: the optical counterpart and redshift credit does not map onto Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni, and an incorrect credit is a lasting mistake. A prize with a defensible two-name credit and reproduced results is better than one that is larger in content but contested in names. On his point about prospective payoffs, I think the millimetre-scale redshift measurements and the constraints on constants are existing results, not promises, so the clock has already shown that it is a new way to observe nature. If expert reports resolve the B038 attribution, I would look at it again, but I would not delay B018 for that.

responses.point: Mehlig asks the committee to separate the lattice concept (Katori) from the accuracy campaign (Ye, with Lemonde, Takamoto and others), and could move to B018 if B012 looks like a sequel to 2016.
responses.response: The separation he asks for is reasonable and I think the citation should make it: the lattice concept and first realisation on one side, the systematic and coherence programme on the other. I would not conclude from that that the second part is only an accuracy record, because the accuracy exists only because someone solved the problems that limited the first generation. His own criterion, a simple and general mechanism, fits the magic wavelength well. On B012 I take the theory seriously, and the mechanism is more compact than most items here. My concern as an experimentalist is the one he raises himself, that first-order melting in some systems qualifies the two-step picture, and with a single first-place vote it would be hard to defend over a case that four members have in their top three.

responses.point: Eriksson finds the B018 attribution persuasive but sees its novelty as closer to 2005 and 2012, a performance record, whereas twisted bilayer graphene revealed a new state of matter.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a new state of matter and a new instrument, but I do not think the prize rules rank them, and the clock is also a discovery about how atoms can be controlled. My reservation on B044 is not the field but the interpretation: with the pairing mechanism unresolved, the citation would have to describe the observation and leave out the physics, and the credit would cost either Bistritzer or the first experimental authors. I keep B044 as my first alternative because I recognise that is a real new-matter case and the experimental reproduction is broad, and I would be willing to revisit it in a few years when the mechanism is clearer.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution, framed as the systematic and coherence programme that made the lattice clock a precision instrument and not as comb infrastructure or a record, is accepted by Olsson, Mehlig and Danielsson as sufficient for a shared prize.
Whether the current record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons are as the files say; I cannot verify them and an expert reviewer should.
Whether the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups are large enough that a two-name credit would be seen as unfair in later years.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes once the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's Boulder laboratory, and Jun Ye worked closely with Hall at JILA; I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I see no specific conflict on B018. I would consider recusal on B023 (close to my rare-earth quantum-information work) and on B008 (I am on the WACQT management team with Goran Johansson), which is why I now list B044 and B008 as alternatives and no longer B023. I would act in discussion on the basis that Johansson recuses on B008 and I do not lead on it.
